title: Resolving Quantum Phase Transitions with Liquid Nitrogen and Liquid Helium Cryogenic S/TEM
content: Strong correlations in quantum materials lead to exotic quantum phases and low-temperature transitions with many real-world applications. Understanding these phases requires disentangling intricate coupling and interplay between structural and electronic degrees of freedom at multiple length scales. In-situ cryogenic scanning transmission electron microscopy (cryo-STEM) is a powerful tool that can probe structural and electronic changes at both atomic and meso- scale across a phase transition allowing access to rich information [1]. For example, charge order in manganites and TaS2 has been extensively studied via liquid nitrogen (LN)-STEM to identify the order parameter and role of defects in emergence of the ordering [2,3]. Due to mechanical instabilities at low temperatures, however, LN-STEM has been limited to techniques with fast acquisition time such as annular dark field (ADF) imaging or lower spatial resolution such as nano-diffraction [1]. With the advances in instrumentation including faster detectors, techniques such as electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) and multislice electron ptychography (MEP) are now possible [4,5]. These advances open new avenues for measuring subtle structural and correlated electronic changes at the highest possible resolution across phase transitions. Along with the development of faster detectors, efforts to attain temperatures lower than LN with liquid Helium (LHe) has attracted great interest [6,7,8]. The ability to reach such low temperatures expands the material space for exploration of novel electron correlations and transitions. Here we leverage recent developments in LN and LHe capabilities to obtain microscopic understanding of low temperature phase transitions in two strongly correlated systems.
